epics.title: Harness fine-tuning pipeline — outstanding work
epics.description:
Capture is built and running; what it stores and why is documented at docs/system-configuration/training-capture.md. Everything downstream of capture is still design.

What we are building and why: fine-tune open models — 8B for the everyday local mind, up to 14B-class where a session warrants — to drive agentic CLI harnesses, meaning correct tool-call syntax, skill invocations, the structural delimiters and stop tokens, and the policy of which tool to reach for in what order against this specific layout, by training on real interaction data captured from the household's own minds. The primary goal is harness fidelity, not reasoning quality: reasoning from a small student will not match a Claude or GPT teacher and that is accepted, because the bottleneck for running a capable local mind on owned hardware is harness behaviour rather than raw intelligence. We are bolting harness-driving competence onto a base model without overwriting its own reasoning or voice. What we are actually building is a tiny model that is a genius inside this specific hive — one that already knows exactly how the day-to-day work here is done, which tools to reach for and in what order against this environment. Not a general assistant; a specialist in operating our world, runnable on owned hardware with no API cost.

Two harnesses are in scope, each its own dataset slice in one shared database: Claude Code, produced by Skippy and Ada with Claude as teacher; and Codex CLI, produced by Nagatha and Mordecai with the Codex model as teacher. This is distillation rather than training a frontier model — the expensive model driving the harness is the teacher and demonstrator, the small open model we own is the student, and nobody is fine-tuning Claude or GPT.

Scope and use, load-bearing for privacy: the trained models, the LoRA weights and the curated training set are internal only — never distributed, sold, shared outside this household's hive, or published, and no commercial use. That makes two things easier. On terms of service, the prohibition on training competing models targets commercial competitive distribution, and internal household use sits outside that surface. On PII, sessions contain household members, friends, medical references and secrets read out of environment files — but because the models never leave the network and the dataset never leaves disk, the threat model collapses to 'what if this machine is compromised', and a compromised box already exposes those files directly, so secrets in training data hand an attacker little they could not already take. Because zero sanitization runs at the start, the no-distribution rule is load-bearing for privacy rather than just licensing: a trained adapter quietly absorbs credentials and personal references in a form harder to audit than a database, which is acceptable as long as the weights never leave the network — and the day anyone proposes distributing or exporting them is the day this and full sanitization must be revisited first. The same caveat extends to any synthetic trajectories.
epics.requirements:
The strategy merge. Two data sources, not two pipelines. Organic capture is ours: real production turns from the minds as they actually work, free because already captured, perfectly matched to real usage distribution — but thin, slow to accumulate, biased toward whatever got done that week, sparse on rare cases, and unable to manufacture coverage of a capability on demand. Synthetic generation is Hermes': run the agent at scale against a curated task list and emit a trajectory per task, with parallel runs over a dataset, checkpoint and resume, ShareGPT-style trajectory emission and per-tool success and failure stats — buying volume, breadth and deliberate targeting of weak spots, but with invented tasks that may drift from how the minds are really used. Neither is superior in the abstract and they are complementary: organic real turns are the high-value core and synthetic generation is the volume multiplier, so the right shape is a hybrid that keeps organic as the truth signal and, when volume runs short, generates synthetic trajectories seeded from our own real task patterns — clustering the recurring sequences already in the turn store, turning each cluster into a task spec, and running the harness against it — so the invented tasks still look like our work. Do not drop organic capture; the hybrid is the design.

Adopt Hermes' downstream machinery wholesale, since we have no consumer for the captured rows and that is the single biggest return gap. Port the trajectory compressor, protecting the head of system plus first request and the tail of final actions while summarizing the middle, so long captured rollouts fit the training context window without losing the opening intent or the closing moves. Adopt the held-out eval discipline so every run measures whether the adapter actually improved before it gets served, which we currently have no gate for. And reuse the dataset assembly step, which assembles rows into a token-budgeted SFT set with a held-out split, as the projection layer over our raw store.

Phasing: now, organic capture plus the ported downstream of compression, eval and assembly, which alone closes the captured-but-never-consumed gap and produces the first real fine-tune; at the volume wall, add synthetic generation seeded from real task clusters as the amplifier, sharing the same recurring-sequence analysis the skill proposer's clustering uses.
epics.acceptance_criteria: Rollout sequence, each step proving the one before it. Capture foundation — done, with the per-turn storage helper redesigned from the session-grain original, the Claude consumer and Skippy's Stop hook registered and validated end to end, the Codex consumer with Mordecai's hook wrapper importing it and runtime verification of live Codex capture pending, and 58 parser, storage and migration tests. Add Ada to the Claude-side capture on the same hook so both feed the Claude slice. Confirm Codex capture end to end on Nagatha and Mordecai after restart. Port the Hermes downstream — compressor, assembly, held-out eval — which is the missing consumer and turns the parked database into a training set, with tests landing with the code. Wire the quality filter, defining what makes a turn training-worthy and populating the quality and judge columns, all pending today, before the first run. First fine-tune at a thousand or more quality-passing tool-call turns, full-from-base LoRA, evaluated against held-out. Then the enrichment fork, adding reasoning provenance and back-filling synthetic rationale grounded in real tool calls. Then the automated loop with its schedule and threshold gate, VRAM eviction and eval-gated adapter swap. And finally synthetic trajectory generation at the volume wall.
epics.qa_tests:
The eval gate is the hard rule: no adapter is swapped into service until it beats the incumbent on held-out tool-call accuracy and format adherence. The held-out set is 100 to 200 turns or sessions never seen in training, checking that tool-call syntax parses by the harness as a structural pass rate, that stop tokens land in the right places with no stream desync, that skill and tool invocations trigger when the prompt warrants, and multi-step task completion on a small fixed set as a sanity check rather than the primary metric.

Four open questions: which 8B to standardize on and whether the fine-tune is served through Ollama as a new tag or a separate runtime; what makes a turn training-worthy, which has to be wired before the first run; a dedup strategy, so near-duplicate tool-call turns of the same tool and shape collapse and the count reflects diversity rather than repetition; and how tightly generated task specs should hew to real clusters before the synthetic trajectories start drifting from real usage.

features.title: Threshold and adapter mechanics
features.description: For a small model we train a low-rank adapter rather than a full fine-tune.
features.requirements:
LoRA versus QLoRA — use plain LoRA at 8B. The only difference is whether the frozen base is quantized: QLoRA squashes it to 4-bit to save VRAM while plain LoRA keeps it at bf16, and both train identical adapters. At 8B on the 48GB A6000 the bf16 base is only about 16GB, so plain LoRA is strictly better — no quantization noise in the frozen base and no on-the-fly dequantization per step. Budget about 2GB per billion parameters, so up to roughly 14B fits as plain LoRA and 20B or more forces QLoRA. Training precision is orthogonal to serving: train the adapter in bf16, then merge and quantize to a q4 GGUF for snappy inference.

Threshold sizing: real behaviour change on tool-call format and harness conventions appears at roughly 500 to 1000 clean diverse examples, with a comfortable first-run target of 1000 to 2000 clean turns. Quality and diversity dominate raw count — a thousand varied clean traces beat ten thousand near-duplicates — and dedup plus quality filtering shaves the usable count, so cross about a thousand good turns before the first run. Current position at the time of writing: 549 tool-call turns, roughly halfway to a solid first adapter pre-filtering. The first-run trigger is a thousand or more quality-passing tool-call turns.

Fine-tune mechanics: supervised fine-tuning via LoRA in standard chat format, with a system prompt and multi-turn messages carrying tool-call and tool-result turns. The loss mask is the key knob — gradients on assistant tool-call spans and turn delimiters only, with user and tool-result tokens as context. Thinking is handled by the export recipe rather than by deletion. A rough run at five thousand examples, three epochs and rank 64 is four to eight hours on the A6000.
features.acceptance_criteria: No adapter is swapped into service until it beats the incumbent on held-out tool-call accuracy and format adherence.
features.qa_tests: The loss mask is the thing most likely to be wrong in a way that still trains: gradients must be on assistant tool-call spans and delimiters only. A run that puts gradients on tool-result tokens teaches the model to produce tool results, which looks like training and is not.

stories.qa_tests: A turn full of failing tool calls does not pass. A clean varied turn does. The count after filtering is what the threshold reads, so an unfiltered count is not the trigger.

stories.description: Near-duplicate tool-call turns of the same tool and shape should collapse. A thousand varied clean traces beat ten thousand near-duplicates.
stories.requirements: Collapsed, not deleted, so the original rows survive.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The usable count is a diversity count.
stories.qa_tests: A set of near-identical turns collapses to one usable example. A set of genuinely varied turns does not collapse.

stories.description: At a thousand or more quality-passing tool-call turns. Plain LoRA at 8B, bf16 frozen base, then merge and quantize to q4 for serving.
stories.requirements: The loss mask on assistant tool-call spans and turn delimiters only.
stories.acceptance_criteria: An adapter that beats the incumbent on held-out tool-call accuracy.
stories.qa_tests: Held-out structural pass rate improves. Stop tokens land correctly with no stream desync. A run with gradients on tool-result tokens trains the wrong thing and is the defect to watch for.

stories.requirements: Both answered.

features.title: Retrain policy — scale-tiered, not one rule
features.description:
Three distinct strategies, often conflated: a full retrain from base on the full accumulated corpus every run; a warm start from the previous adapter still training on the full corpus; and true incremental or continual training, continuing the previous adapter on only the new slice.

The third is the trap and is rejected outright. Training on only-new rows causes catastrophic forgetting, because weights slide toward the newest batch and erode the rare tool-call patterns we care most about — rare data is overwritten first — and irreproducibility, because the model becomes an order-dependent chain you cannot rebuild, bisect, or back a bad batch out of. Forgetting is caused by starving the model of old data rather than by continuing from a previous model, and that distinction is what makes the tiers work.
features.requirements:
Tier 1, small data and where we are: rebuild the adapter from base on the full corpus every run. The dataset is the source of truth and the adapter is a disposable derived artifact, so every model is a pure function of the database right now, reproducible, and a bad batch is one delete from gone. LoRA on a few-thousand-example 8B corpus is cheap — tens of minutes to one or two hours on the A6000. The graduation trigger is wall-clock rather than row count: training time scales roughly linearly with rows times epochs, bending slightly sub-linear since large sets need fewer epochs, and the operational constraint is the overnight window of the 02:00 job at about five or six hours. So as long as a full-from-base retrain finishes inside that window, keep doing full retrains, because it is strictly cleaner — and that holds comfortably past ten thousand rows, a year or more out at current capture. Tier 1 runs the show for a long time and is not a stopgap.

Tier 2, when a full retrain exceeds the overnight window at roughly ten to thirty thousand rows: periodic rebase plus replay. Most cycles are a continued run from the current adapter on new rows plus a replay sample of older rows — never only-new, because replay tames forgetting at scale — at a low learning rate for one or two epochs. Periodically, monthly or on a base-model or schema change, one clean full retrain from base cuts the dependency chain and restores reproducibility. There is an adapter wrinkle: a single low-rank adapter saturates its rank if trained forever, so either merge into base and start fresh or let the monthly full rebase reset it — and since serving is quantized, each merge-and-requantize adds noise, which is another reason the periodic clean rebase is hygiene.

Tier 3, when a full retrain exceeds a day at a hundred thousand rows or more: continued-with-replay becomes the everyday path and full rebase becomes a rare triggered event on a base-model change, a schema change, or quarterly. This is where a second or larger GPU stops being a luxury.
features.acceptance_criteria: The bottom line: we can build on previously trained models, but it is a tier we graduate into with replay and periodic rebases rather than the starting policy. At our size, full-from-base every run is correct and stays correct for a long time.
features.qa_tests: Reproducibility is the property Tier 1 buys and the thing to verify: the same database state produces the same adapter, so a bad batch can be deleted and the adapter rebuilt. Once that stops holding, the tier has changed.

stories.title: Keep full-from-base retrains while they fit the overnight window
stories.description: Tier 1. The dataset is the source of truth and the adapter is a disposable derived artifact. The graduation trigger is wall-clock rather than row count.
stories.requirements: Full corpus, every run, from base.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Every model is a pure function of the database, and a bad batch is one delete from gone.
stories.qa_tests: A rebuild from the same database state reproduces the adapter. Deleting a batch and rebuilding removes its influence entirely — which only holds in this tier.

stories.title: Add replay sampling for the Tier 2 graduation
stories.description: When a full retrain exceeds the overnight window. Continued runs on new rows plus a replay sample of older rows, never only-new, at a low learning rate for one or two epochs — with a periodic clean full rebase from base to cut the dependency chain.
stories.requirements: Replay in every continued run; a periodic rebase for hygiene.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Rare tool-call patterns survive, because they are the first thing only-new training overwrites.
stories.qa_tests: A continued run with replay retains held-out performance on rare patterns; one without it does not, which is the measurement that justifies the replay. The adapter's rank saturation is the second reason for the rebase — a merge-and-requantize each cycle adds noise.

features.title: Thinking-enrichment fork
features.description:
The corpus has almost no reasoning — two rows of 565. Back-fill it so the data teaches why a tool was called rather than only which. Generate synthetic rationale for each tool-call turn using strong local reasoning models.

The critical grounding rule: condition the generator on the tool call that actually happened, reverse-rationalizing from the known-correct action. Never generate rationale blind and staple the real call on afterwards, or you train the model to hallucinate justifications. Grounding in the real outcome produces a genuine decision process.

Recursive capture: while the enrichment models reason, capture their thinking as additional training data.

This is distinct from synthetic trajectory generation — enrichment fills in rationale for real tool calls, while synthetic generation manufactures whole new task trajectories for volume. Both carry explicit provenance and both live under the internal-only scope.
features.requirements: Provenance is mandatory: add a reasoning-source column distinguishing real from synthetic-with-the-model-named, so human-grounded tool calls and machine reasoning are never blended indiscriminately. The existing has-reasoning flag is the start; the source column is the needed extension. This applies beyond Codex — Claude rows carry encrypted thinking and Codex rows carry zero thinking, and both benefit.
features.acceptance_criteria: No rationale enters the corpus without its provenance recorded.
features.qa_tests: The grounding rule is the one with a training-level failure behind it: rationale generated blind and stapled to a real call teaches the model to invent justifications, which is worse than no rationale at all. So the test is that the generator's input includes the actual tool call.

stories.title: Add the reasoning-source column
stories.description: real, or synthetic with the generating model named. So human-grounded tool calls and machine reasoning are never blended indiscriminately.
stories.requirements: Mandatory on every enriched row.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Provenance is queryable.
stories.qa_tests: An enriched row carries its source. A row without one is not assemblable into a dataset.

stories.title: Generate rationale grounded in the tool call that actually happened
stories.description: Reverse-rationalize from the known-correct action. Never generate blind and staple the real call on after.
stories.requirements: The generator is conditioned on the real call.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The rationale explains the action that was taken.
stories.qa_tests: The generator's input includes the actual tool call. Blind generation plus a stapled call would pass a shape check and teach the model to hallucinate justifications, which is the failure this rule exists for.

stories.title: Capture the enrichment models' own thinking
stories.description: Recursive capture: while the enrichment models reason, their thinking is additional training data.
stories.requirements: Captured under the same provenance discipline.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The enrichment pass produces data as well as consuming it.
stories.qa_tests: An enrichment run produces rows carrying its own model as the source.

features.title: The automated loop
features.description: Scheduled, for example Wednesday at 02:00, and gated by the threshold — only fire if enough new quality rows landed since the last run. Schedule and threshold, both.
features.requirements: VRAM handling on a 48GB card: the classifier alone is about 14GB resident, and an 8B plain-LoRA job with a bf16 frozen base wants 20 to 24GB. Do not kill the Ollama daemon — evict its models for the training window, either with a stop command or by zeroing the keep-alive, run training, and let the models reload on the next request. At 02:00 only background sweeps might touch them, and they tolerate a short pause. The run then rebuilds the adapter from base on the full filtered corpus, validates against held-out, swaps the served adapter only if it wins, and reloads the models. Reuse the existing scheduler — the same surface as the nightly job — rather than a new daemon.
features.acceptance_criteria: The adapter swap is eval-gated, so a worse adapter never reaches service.
features.qa_tests: The eviction path matters because killing the daemon is the obvious wrong move: models must reload on the next request rather than needing a restart. The gate is testable with a deliberately worse adapter, which must not be swapped in.

stories.title: Schedule the run with a threshold gate
stories.description: Both: a cadence, and a minimum of new quality rows since the last run. Reuse the existing scheduler rather than a new daemon.
stories.requirements: No run on a quiet week.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A week with too few new quality rows does not train.
stories.qa_tests: With insufficient new rows, no run fires. With enough, one does.

stories.title: Evict Ollama's models for the training window rather than killing the daemon
stories.description: A stop command or a zeroed keep-alive. The models reload on the next request.
stories.requirements: The daemon stays up.
stories.acceptance_criteria: VRAM is free for the job and the models come back by themselves.
stories.qa_tests: After eviction, the resident footprint drops and a subsequent request reloads the model with no restart. Killing the daemon would also free the memory and is the wrong move, because nothing brings it back.

stories.title: Gate the adapter swap on beating the incumbent
stories.description: Validate against held-out and swap only if it wins.
stories.requirements: The incumbent is the baseline, not an absolute score.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A worse adapter never reaches service.
stories.qa_tests: A deliberately worse adapter is not swapped in. A better one is. The held-out set is never seen in training, which is what makes the comparison meaningful.

features.title: Episodes — distillation and meta-learning
features.description:
Curation as built is per-turn: the turn store carries a session id and a turn index so ordering exists, but nothing groups a contiguous span of turns into one job attempted and eventually completed. Two things we want are inexpressible over a single turn and both need the same missing primitive. Distillation boils the many turns that achieved a goal down to the short path that achieved it. Meta-learning takes an episode with false starts, wrong locations, a correction from the operator, and a correct ending, and derives how this job should be approached. The prerequisite for both is an episode layer — a span with a goal, an outcome and a boundary. One table and a detector.

Ordering matters, because curation would destroy the meta-learning input. The curation pass excludes tool-error-dominant, interrupted and harness-error rows, on the correct reasoning that a turn full of failing tool calls teaches flailing. That is right for per-turn SFT and fatal for meta-learning, because the false start IS the signal — the lesson 'do not start in the wrong location' is only derivable from the turn that started in the wrong location. So the pass order is fixed: assemble episodes, extract from the whole episode garbage included, and only then apply per-turn exclusion to what gets emitted as trainable rows. Bolting distillation on after the existing filter deletes its own raw material.

One episode yields three artifacts. A distilled trajectory — the short clean path, SFT data in the same format as today at a fraction of the tokens, which goes in weights. A prose lesson — 'for this job, do X before Y' — which goes in a skill, a hook or retrieval rather than in weights, because most meta-learning belongs in orchestration, and the same lesson can go both places with the comparison telling us which mechanism actually works. And a preference pair, with the false-start path rejected and the corrected path chosen, which is DPO or ORPO data. The third is the highest-value asset in the corpus and nothing currently reads it: synthetic negatives are invented and weak, while the operator typing 'no, stop, go back' is a gold human label on a bad trajectory, produced free during real work — and correction episodes are the only place real paired negatives exist.
features.requirements:
How to distill, in increasing order of judgment, run in this order because each is cheaper and more verifiable than the next. Trajectory compression: protect head and tail, compress the middle to a token budget — structural, no judgment, blunt. Dependency pruning: given the episode's final successful state, ask which tool calls contributed to it, so a read of the wrong directory whose output is never referenced again gets cut while a read whose content appears in a later edit stays — this is graph reachability over the tool trace rather than summarization, which makes it verifiable, because the pruned trajectory must still reach the same end state. And teacher rewrite, only on what survives pruning, where the teacher emits the idealized path — which is where the judge verdict and confidence columns finally get written, reserved at capture and never yet populated by anything.

The promotion gate is for meta-lessons only. A distilled trajectory needs no gate, because it is validated by the fact that its episode succeeded. A meta-lesson claims generality, so before it may change a skill or enter the training set it must be seen in at least three episodes across more than one session, have a high success rate with no unresolved contradiction with an existing lesson, not be a transient fact or sensitive, be likely to remain valid, and be expressible as a behaviour or a demonstration. The promotion states run observed, repeated, validated, distilled, approved, trained, evaluated, deployed, and then retired or retained.

Keep facts out of weights. The governing rule: if it could change tomorrow and should be edited as a database record, it belongs in memory; if it should consistently alter how the agent approaches similar future tasks, it is a training candidate. Never trainable regardless of how often it recurs: credentials and keys, hostnames and IPs, temporary URLs, current deployment or configuration state, ticket status, calendar entries, personnel assignments, one-off incidents and their workarounds, unconfirmed claims, anything requiring precise deletion, anything that must be retrieved verbatim, and anything with uncertain provenance. That deny-list already matches the ephemeral and secret data classes.
features.acceptance_criteria: The hindsight risk, and its mitigations. Distillation trains on hindsight — the idealized path already knows where the file was — so training exclusively on distilled episodes produces a model that goes straight to the answer without ever having learned to look, and it will go straight to the wrong answer with equal confidence when the situation differs. Mitigations: keep the searches that legitimately narrowed the space and prune only the ones that were wrong; hold back a fraction of undistilled episodes in the mix; mix new distilled examples with a replay set of previously approved ones, starting around 20 to 40 percent new against 60 to 80 percent replay and tuning empirically; and keep a frozen gold set that predates the distillation work, so an adapter is never graded against the same distribution it was trained on.
features.qa_tests: Dependency pruning is verifiable in a way the other two are not: the pruned trajectory must still reach the same end state, which is a checkable property rather than a judgement. The frozen gold set is what keeps the evaluation honest, because grading an adapter against the same distribution it was trained on measures nothing.

stories.title: Add the episode table and a boundary detector
stories.description: A span with a goal, an outcome and a boundary. One table and a detector. The prerequisite for both distillation and meta-learning.
stories.requirements: Assembled before curation runs, because curation deletes the meta-learning input.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A contiguous span of turns is addressable as one job.
stories.qa_tests: An episode's turns include the tool-error-dominant and interrupted ones that per-turn curation excludes, since the false start is the signal. Running curation first and distilling after would pass a shape check and have destroyed its own raw material.

stories.title: Implement dependency pruning over the tool trace
stories.description: Given the episode's final successful state, keep the tool calls that contributed to it. Graph reachability rather than summarization, which is what makes it verifiable.
stories.requirements: The pruned trajectory must still reach the same end state.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A read of the wrong directory whose output is never referenced again is cut; a read whose content appears in a later edit stays.
stories.qa_tests: The pruned trajectory reaches the same end state as the original — a checkable property rather than a judgement. A pruning that drops a contributing call fails it.

stories.title: Emit the three artifacts per episode
stories.description: A distilled trajectory for weights, a prose lesson for a skill, hook or retrieval, and a preference pair with the false start rejected and the correction chosen. The preference pair is the highest-value asset in the corpus and nothing currently reads it.
stories.requirements: All three, with the same lesson allowed to go to both weights and orchestration so the comparison tells us which mechanism works.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A messy episode that eventually succeeded produces all three.
stories.qa_tests: A correction episode produces a pair whose rejected branch is the false start and whose chosen branch is the correction. The operator typing 'no, stop, go back' is a gold human label — synthetic negatives are invented and weak, so a pipeline that manufactures negatives instead of mining corrections has missed the point.

stories.title: Enforce the promotion gate for meta-lessons
stories.description: A distilled trajectory needs no gate, because its episode succeeded. A meta-lesson claims generality: three episodes across more than one session, a high success rate, no unresolved contradiction, not transient, not sensitive, likely to remain valid, and expressible as a behaviour or a demonstration.
stories.requirements: The nine promotion states, tracked.
stories.acceptance_criteria: No lesson changes a skill or enters the training set ungated.
stories.qa_tests: A lesson seen in two episodes does not promote. One seen in three across two sessions does. A lesson contradicting an existing one is held rather than promoted.

stories.title: Enforce the facts-out-of-weights deny-list
stories.description: Credentials and keys, hostnames and IPs, temporary URLs, current deployment or configuration state, ticket status, calendar entries, personnel assignments, one-off incidents and their workarounds, unconfirmed claims, anything requiring precise deletion, anything that must be retrieved verbatim, and anything with uncertain provenance. The list already matches the ephemeral and secret data classes.
stories.requirements: The governing rule: if it could change tomorrow and should be edited as a database record it belongs in memory; if it should consistently alter how the agent approaches similar tasks it is a training candidate.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Nothing on the deny-list reaches a distilled example.
stories.qa_tests: An example containing a credential, a hostname or a ticket status is refused. The ephemeral data class is a discard signal, so a pipeline writing one is a defect rather than an oversight.

stories.title: Mitigate the hindsight risk in the training mix
stories.description: Keep the searches that legitimately narrowed the space and prune only the wrong ones; hold back a fraction of undistilled episodes; mix 20 to 40 percent new distilled examples against 60 to 80 percent replay, tuned empirically; and keep a frozen gold set predating the distillation work.
stories.requirements: All four, because distillation alone trains a model that never learned to look.
stories.acceptance_criteria: An adapter is never graded against the same distribution it was trained on.
stories.qa_tests: The frozen gold set predates the distillation work, so it measures generalisation rather than fit. An adapter trained only on distilled episodes goes straight to the wrong answer with equal confidence when the situation differs, which is the behaviour to watch for on the gold set.

features.title: Corpus measurement — a conversation is not a session
features.description:
Measured 2026-08-06. The turn store's session id is the harness session id, and rotation mints a new one every time the context window crosses the threshold, so a single conversation spans five, ten or a hundred sessions. Measured naively the corpus looks like 6,974 sessions averaging 1.45 turns — an artifact rather than a fact.

The chain is reconstructible: the turn store's session id joins the comms store's harness session id, and from there the session's own id plus the owner triple ordered by creation time gives the conversation. The explicit successor link is populated on only 18 rows, because the migration is recent and terminal rotations respawn in place without creating a successor row — so the owner triple plus creation order is the reliable key rather than the successor link.

Stitched, the corpus looks completely different: Skippy on Telegram accounts for 906 turns across 150 sessions with 101 corrections and 8,984 tool calls; Skippy on web and terminal for 485 turns across 78 sessions with 59 corrections and 5,490 tool calls; three others for 120 turns across 19 sessions with 6 corrections and 481 tool calls — totalling 1,511 turns joined to a real conversation, 166 corrections and 14,955 tool calls. The other roughly 8,600 turns join no comms session at all: they are scheduler and hook one-shots, including 155 identical README-audit prompts and a long tail of reminder-check and alerter fires, one turn each. The presence of a comms session row is a better conversational filter than turn count — 52 percent of multi-turn harness sessions join, against 0.7 percent of single-turn ones. So the conversational corpus is about 15 percent of the rows and carries essentially all of the tool-call density and every correction, and two conversations dominate it.
features.requirements:
The remaining problem is segmentation rather than stitching. Those two conversations are owner-lifetime buckets — months of work in one stream — rather than episodes, and an episode is a sub-span. Rotation boundaries are a usable first proxy at about six turns per rotated session, a plausible episode size, but rotation fires on context percentage rather than goal completion so a job routinely straddles one. Segmenting the 906-turn stream into jobs is the actual open work.

There is a useful coincidence: the rotation harvest already classifies and distills at every boundary, and its output is a per-boundary summary of what the span was about, which is exactly the signal a segmenter needs and is already being written to memory. But measured, it does not segment yet. The harvest is not on the session row — the row's summary is the verbatim opening user message and its carry-forward is transient, with none of the 150 rows in the Telegram chain holding one. It is in lucent as rotation-sourced memories: 654 records across 295 rotation events for Skippy, each carrying a project line, a goal, what was in flight and a next step. Every record parses and every record carries a project slug — but there are 637 distinct slugs across 654 records, and exactly one project appears in three or more rotation events. The harvest mints a fresh name each time for work that is often the same ongoing job, so the labels are high quality per event and useless as identifiers. Grouping sessions by slug equality recovers nothing.

Two ways forward, not exclusive: cluster the slug plus goal text semantically to recover episode identity after the fact, or fix the harvest to carry the prior slug forward when the work continues instead of naming it again. The second is cheaper, makes every future rotation self-segmenting, and is worth doing whether or not the distillation pipeline gets built.

Session boundaries alone do not segment either, in both directions: of 149 boundaries in the Telegram chain, 49 have a sub-two-minute gap — rotation cutting a job in half, or image-heavy turns burning context one message at a time — while single sessions of 20 or more turns routinely span several unrelated topics.
features.acceptance_criteria: Four open questions. Episode boundary detection: the conversation chain is solved and goal boundaries are not, with candidate signals being rotation-harvest summaries as span labels, operator correction markers, tool-error-ratio spikes, a restated goal, and long idle gaps in the capture timestamps. Volume: 166 corrections inside 1,391 conversational turns across two conversations is enough to hand-review and not enough to justify a nightly pipeline, so build the extractor against these by hand first. Retention: 8,600 captured turns no longer join any session row, so if conversational context is wanted for older turns, the comms session rows must outlive the conversation or the gateway id must be stamped onto the turn at capture time. And where the prose lesson lands: skill text, a prompt hook, or a retrieval entry — and whether the weights version ever beats the retrieval version.
features.qa_tests: The slug measurement is the finding that matters: 637 distinct slugs across 654 records means grouping by slug equality recovers nothing, so a segmenter built on slug equality would silently produce one episode per rotation. The sub-two-minute-gap count shows the reverse error too — rotation boundaries both over- and under-segment.

stories.title: Fix the harvest to carry the prior slug forward when work continues
stories.description: Cheaper than semantic clustering, makes every future rotation self-segmenting, and is worth doing whether or not the distillation pipeline gets built. Today the harvest mints a fresh name each time for work that is often the same ongoing job — 637 distinct slugs across 654 records, with exactly one project appearing in three or more events.
stories.requirements: Carry the prior slug when the work continues rather than naming it again.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Grouping by slug equality recovers real episodes.
stories.qa_tests: A continuing job produces the same slug across consecutive rotation events. Two eight-minutes-apart events on one job no longer carry two names.

stories.title: Cluster slug and goal text semantically to recover past episode identity
stories.description: For the corpus already captured, where the slugs are already useless as identifiers. Not exclusive with fixing the harvest.
stories.requirements: Recovers episode identity after the fact.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The 906-turn Telegram stream segments into jobs.
stories.qa_tests: Clustering groups the known-same jobs together. Slug equality alone recovers nothing, which is the baseline to beat.

stories.title: Build the correction extractor by hand against the 166 known corrections
stories.description: Enough to hand-review, not enough to justify a nightly pipeline. Two conversations carry essentially all the tool-call density and every correction.
stories.requirements: Built against the real corrections first.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Preference pairs come out of real operator corrections.
stories.qa_tests: Each extracted pair's rejected branch is a real false start and its chosen branch the real correction, verified by reading. 166 is a hand-reviewable number, which is why this precedes automation.

stories.title: Decide retention for turns that join no session row
stories.description: 8,600 captured turns no longer join any session row. If conversational context is wanted for older turns, the comms session rows must outlive the conversation, or the gateway id must be stamped onto the turn at capture time.
stories.requirements: A decision, and the stamp if that is the answer.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Future turns are joinable.
stories.qa_tests: A newly captured turn carries enough to reconstruct its conversation after the session row is gone. Stamping at capture time is the forward fix; the 8,600 already captured are not recoverable either way.

stories.title: Decide where the prose lesson lands and whether weights ever beat retrieval
stories.description: Skill text, a prompt hook, or a retrieval entry. The same lesson can go both places, and comparing the two tells us which mechanism actually works.
stories.requirements: Both placements tried, and compared.
stories.acceptance_criteria: An answer about which mechanism works.
stories.qa_tests: The same lesson in weights and in retrieval is compared on the same held-out tasks. Most meta-learning belongs in orchestration, so the retrieval version winning is the expected result rather than a disappointment.

features.title: Capture foundation and the remaining capture work
features.description: Steps 1 through 3 of the rollout. The foundation is done; two pieces of capture remain.
features.requirements: The storage helper writes per-turn rows, redesigned from the session-grain original. The Claude consumer and Skippy's Stop hook are registered and validated end to end. The Codex consumer exists and Mordecai's hook wrapper imports it, with runtime verification of live Codex capture pending. 58 parser, storage and migration tests. The per-turn redesign shipped with a data contract document and a migration script.
features.acceptance_criteria: Ada added to the Claude-side capture on the same hook so Skippy and Ada both feed the Claude slice, and Codex capture confirmed end to end on Nagatha and Mordecai after restart — at which point it stops being a Codex blocker.
features.qa_tests: The Codex confirmation is a runtime verification rather than a test: new turns have to appear. Note that Nagatha lacks the training-capture hook entirely, which is its own gap.

stories.title: Build the per-turn capture foundation
stories.description: DONE. The storage helper writing per-turn rows, the Claude consumer, Skippy's Stop hook registered and validated end to end, the Codex consumer with Mordecai's wrapper importing it, 58 tests, a data contract document and a migration script.
stories.requirements: Per-turn grain, redesigned from the session-grain original.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Capture is running.
stories.qa_tests: Covered by the 58 parser, storage and migration tests.

stories.title: Add Ada to the Claude-side capture
stories.description: The same hook, so Skippy and Ada both feed the Claude slice.
stories.requirements: One hook, two minds.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Ada's turns appear in the Claude slice.
stories.qa_tests: A turn of Ada's produces a row carrying her own mind id rather than Skippy's.

stories.title: Confirm Codex capture end to end on Nagatha and Mordecai
stories.description: Runtime verification pending. It stops being a Codex blocker once new turns verify. Nagatha lacks the training-capture hook entirely, which has to be fixed first.
stories.requirements: The hook present on both, then new turns verified.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Live Codex turns are captured.
stories.qa_tests: A real Codex turn produces a row. Nagatha's missing hook is the first thing to check, since a confirmation run against a mind with no hook proves nothing.

features.title: Related direction — a containerized Skippy
features.description:
Under discussion, not decided at the time of writing. A second Skippy that is the same mind — same soul, same lucent memory — but running as a container in the hive-mind compose layout rather than bare-metal systemd, given host Docker socket access and broad host bind-mounts so it keeps the systemd Skippy's full reach while conforming to the standard mind-container layout. Continuity is safe because identity lives in the knowledge graph and vector store rather than on container disk.

The honest caveat: such a container is privileged by design — a host Docker socket plus a root bind-mount is host-equivalent, so 'sandbox' no longer applies and mounts should be scoped deliberately. It also shifts the captured training distribution toward container-shaped tool calls, which for a model meant to drive this hive is arguably the right distribution to learn. Captured so the decision is made with eyes open.
features.requirements: A decision, with the privilege acknowledged rather than glossed.
features.acceptance_criteria: Mordecai has since shipped as exactly this shape — a container with a single host mount and a home symlink, operator-mind pattern — so the pattern is proven even if a containerized Skippy is not built.
features.qa_tests: The distribution shift is the interesting consequence rather than a risk: a model meant to drive this hive learning container-shaped tool calls is arguably correct, which is a judgement to make deliberately rather than discover in the corpus.

stories.title: Decide whether Skippy is containerized
stories.description: Same soul, same memory, container layout, privileged by design. The pattern is proven by Mordecai; what is undecided is whether Skippy moves. Note the operating rule that follows: a mind must not bounce its own container.
stories.requirements: The privilege acknowledged, and mounts scoped deliberately.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A decision made with eyes open.
stories.qa_tests: Not code. If it proceeds, continuity is verified by the mind answering with its own identity from the knowledge graph rather than from container disk.
